intro: After the five books of the Torah, the Bible tells a long story in order. A people crosses a river into a land. Leaders rise up when there is trouble. Then the people ask for a king. This unit follows that story through the books of Joshua, Judges, Ruth, Samuel and the first part of Kings. Jewish readers call most of these books the Former Prophets. Christian readers call them the Historical Books.

You will meet Joshua at Jericho and Deborah under her palm tree. You will meet Gideon with three hundred men and Samson with his uncut hair. You will walk with Ruth from Moab to Bethlehem. You will watch Samuel anoint Saul and then David. You will see David face a giant, become a king and make a terrible mistake. You will hear Solomon judge two mothers and build a Temple. Then you will see his kingdom split in two.

Along the way you will learn what a judge was and what a covenant is. You will learn what the text says a king was supposed to do. You will read short passages from the King James Version and put them in your own words. And you will practice a skill that matters for the whole course. Say what a story says. Say how its readers have read it. Do not decide for anyone what to believe.
bigQuestion: What do the stories of the judges and the first kings show about what their readers valued in a leader?

timeline.t: The book of Joshua sets the crossing of the Jordan and the fall of Jericho around this time, as many scholars date the story
The period of the judges begins: Deborah, Gideon, Samson and others, as the book of Judges tells it
The book of Ruth is set in the days of the judges, in Bethlehem and Moab
Samuel anoints Saul, the first king, according to 1 Samuel
David becomes king and makes Jerusalem his capital
Solomon builds the First Temple in Jerusalem, as 1 Kings describes
The kingdom splits into Israel in the north and Judah in the south
Assyria conquers the northern kingdom of Israel
Babylon captures Jerusalem and destroys the First Temple
The King James Version, which this unit quotes, is printed in England
The Jewish Publication Society prints its English Tanakh

words.d: the Jewish name for Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings
the Christian name for Joshua through Esther, which tell a story in order
a very large family group with its own name; the Bible counts twelve tribes of Israel
a binding promise with rules on both sides; in the Hebrew Bible, the bond between God and Israel
in the book of Judges, a leader who rises up to rescue the people in a time of trouble
a person who speaks a message from God, such as Deborah, Samuel or Nathan
a Hebrew word for loyal kindness that goes beyond what is required; the main idea of Ruth
gathering leftover grain after the harvest, which the Torah says must be left for the poor and the stranger
to pour oil on a person's head as a sign that they are chosen for a job, such as king
a short story that teaches by making the listener see something in a new way
the house of worship Solomon built in Jerusalem, where the priests served and the ark was kept
after the split, the southern kingdom with Jerusalem and the Temple

test.q: Which book comes first in this unit's story?
test.why: Joshua follows Deuteronomy and tells of crossing the Jordan. Judges, Ruth and Samuel come after.

test.q: What does the word judge mean in the book of Judges?
choices: A leader who rises up in a crisis
A person who copies the law
test.why: Judges are rescuers raised up in trouble, such as Deborah and Gideon, not courtroom officials.

test.q: What does the last verse of Judges say?
choices: There was no king, and everyone did what was right in their own eyes
test.why: Judges 21:25 closes the book with this line. Many readers see it as a hint that a king is coming.

test.q: Who said, Where you go, I will go?
test.why: Ruth 1:16 gives Ruth's promise to her mother-in-law Naomi on the road to Bethlehem.

test.q: Which tribe held no land of its own and served at the place of worship?
test.why: Joshua 21 says the Levites lived in towns spread among the other tribes.

test.q: Who was the mother who prayed at Shiloh for a son?
test.why: 1 Samuel 1 tells of Hannah's prayer. Her son was Samuel.

test.q: What did Samuel warn a king would do?
choices: Take sons, daughters, fields and a tenth of the grain
test.why: 1 Samuel 8 lists what a king will take from the people. They asked for a king anyway.

test.q: What did David use against Goliath?
test.why: 1 Samuel 17 says David took off Saul's armor and went out with a sling and five smooth stones.

test.q: Who was David's closest friend, the son of King Saul?
test.why: Jonathan protected David from his father's jealousy. Nathan was a prophet and Boaz married Ruth.

test.q: What did David do at Jerusalem after he captured it?
choices: He brought the ark there and made it his capital
He gave it to the Philistines
test.why: 2 Samuel 5 and 6 tell how David made Jerusalem his capital and brought the ark. Solomon built the Temple.

test.q: How do Jewish and Christian traditions differ in reading the promise to David in 2 Samuel 7?
choices: Jewish tradition hopes for a future king from David's line; Christian tradition says Jesus is that king
Both say Solomon was that king and the promise ended
test.why: Both traditions read the same chapter as a promise about David's line, but they differ on who fulfills it.

test.q: Why did Nathan tell David a story about a lamb?
choices: To explain the rules for sacrifice
To lead David to judge his own wrong
test.why: 2 Samuel 12: David condemned the rich man, and Nathan said, You are the man.

test.q: What did Solomon ask for in his dream at Gibeon?
choices: An understanding heart to judge the people
test.why: 1 Kings 3 says Solomon asked for wisdom to judge. The text says riches and honor were added.

test.q: About when do many scholars place the split of the kingdom?
test.why: The split after Solomon's death is usually placed around 930 BCE. 722 and 586 BCE are the falls of Israel and Judah.

test.q: What was Deuteronomy 17's test for a king, which the books of Kings use for every ruler?
choices: Did he keep the covenant and the law?
test.why: Deuteronomy 17 says a king must read the law daily and keep it. Kings gives each ruler a short report on that.

write.prompt: What did these books say a good leader was? Choose two or three passages from the unit, such as Joshua 1:9, Judges 21:25, Ruth 1:16, 1 Samuel 16:7 or 1 Kings 3:9. Say what each passage says about a leader. Then explain how Jewish readers, Christian readers or scholars have read it. Use your own words.
tips: Name each passage by book, chapter and verse.
Say the story says or the text says. Do not tell the reader what to believe.
When you describe a belief, say whose it is: Jewish tradition, Christian tradition, many scholars.
Compare two readings instead of picking a winner.
Use the unit's words: judge, covenant, anoint, prophet, hesed.
